extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent attorneys/agents; patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed inventions meet 35 U.S.C. §101 subject matter eligibility using the USPTO two-step analysis (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: judicial exceptions and inventive concept). Intended to guide examination practice and record-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step subject matter eligibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two criteria for determining subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 and both must be satisfied: (1) the claimed invention must be directed to one of the four statutory categories, and (2) the claimed invention must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The following two-step analysis is used to evaluate these criteria. Both criteria must be met for patent eligibility. (Original phrasing: 'The claimed invention (1) must be directed to one of the four statutory categories, and (2) must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category requirement (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to one of the four patent-eligible subject matter categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter? The subject matter of the claim must be directed to one of the four subject matter categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is not, the claim is not eligible for patent protection and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If the claim plainly fails Step 1 but could be amended to fall within a statutory category, Step 2 should still be conducted. Use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification and one skilled in the art when determining whether a claim encompasses non-statutory embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Process — an act, or a series of acts or steps. (Quoted: 'A process is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result. It is an act, or a series of acts, performed upon the subject-matter to be transformed and reduced to a different state or thing.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law examples cited: Gottschalk v. Benson; NTP, Inc. v. Research in Motion; Minton v. Natl. Ass’n. of Securities Dealers. See also 35 U.S.C. 100(b) and Bilski v. Kappos. Use these authorities to characterize claimed methods/processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine — a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices. Includes mechanical devices or combinations of mechanical powers and devices to perform some function and produce a certain effect or result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law example cited: Burr v. Duryee; Corning v. Burden. Treat claimed apparatus or device combinations as machines when concrete physical parts are recited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacture — an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving to these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations, whether by hand labor or by machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law example cited: Diamond v. Chakrabarty (quoting Am. Fruit Growers v. Brogdex). Use this standard when the claimed subject is an article created from materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of matter — all compositions of two or more substances and all composite articles, whether the results of chemical union or mechanical mixture, or gases, fluids, powders or solids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law example cited: Chakrabarty. Apply when claims recite chemical or material compositions or composite articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory examples (items that are not directed to statutory categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to one of the statutory categories include: (i) transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., a propagating electrical or electromagnetic signal per se), (ii) a human per se, (iii) a legal contractual agreement between two parties, (iv) a computer program per se, (v) a company, (vi) a mere arrangement of printed matter, and (vii) data per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: In re Nuijten; AIA; In re Ferguson; Gottschalk v. Benson; In re Miller; Digitech Image Tech. If the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim encompasses such non-statutory embodiments, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Example: machine-readable media that can encompass a carrier wave or transitory signal should be rejected if BRI includes the transitory form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — Judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2: Does the claim wholly embrace a judicially recognized exception, which includes laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas? Claims directed to nothing more than abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and laws of nature are not eligible for patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedents: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank; Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad; Bilski v. Kappos; Diamond v. Diehr; Parker v. Flook; Gottschalk v. Benson. The guidance notes that the exceptions have also been described by other terms (e.g., 'physical phenomena,' 'scientific principles,' 'mental processes,' 'disembodied mathematical algorithms'). Use these authorities to identify judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether the elements of the claim, considered both individually and as an ordered combination, are sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception itself — i.e., whether there is an 'inventive concept.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analysis asks whether the claim is for a particular application of an abstract idea/natural phenomenon or is the abstract idea/natural phenomenon itself. Authorities: Alice Corp.; Mayo Collaborative Serv. v. Prometheus; Diehr. Methods and products employing exceptions to perform a real-world function may still be patentable if the claim as a whole is 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case requirement and burden shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel should review the totality of the evidence (specification, claims, relevant prior art) and must reach a conclusion whether it is more likely than not that the claimed invention either falls outside one of the enumerated statutory classes or within one of the judicial exceptions. The examiner bears the initial burden of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: In re Oetiker (examiner initial burden), In re Brana (burden shifts to applicant after examiner explains why claim is an exception without significantly more). If the record suggests the claim is 'significantly more' than an exception, examiners should not reject. After identifying and explaining reasons the claim is for an exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to applicant to amend or show eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that encompass both statutory and non-statutory embodiments fail Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (under the broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification and one skilled in the art) embraces non-statutory subject matter and therefore fails Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a computer readable medium claim that can be a compact disc (statutory) or a carrier wave (transitory, non-statutory) — under BRI such a claim covers a non-statutory embodiment and should be rejected. Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 when making such rejections and consult MPEP § 706.03(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete examination and compact prosecution obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under the other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and utility, inventorship, double patenting, and non-statutory double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action (compact prosecution). Even if a 101 rejection is made, include other applicable rejections so the record is complete.
